title: Plato’s precious stones and the city in Isaiah
source_text: Δοκεῖ δέ μοι καὶ τὰ περὶ τῶν τῇδε τιμίων εἶναι νομιζομένων λίθων, ἀποῤῥοήν τινα λεγομένων ἔχειν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῇ κρείττονι γῇ λίθων, εἰλῆφθαι τῷ Πλάτωνι ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ ἀναγεγραμμένων περὶ τῆς πόλεως τοῦ θεοῦ. περὶ ἧς γέγραπται· „θήσω τὰς ἐπάλξεις σου ἴασπιν καὶ τοὺς λίθους σου λίθους κρυστάλλου καὶ τὸν περίβολόν σου λίθους ἐκλεκτοὺς“ καὶ πάλιν· „θήσω τὰ θεμέλιά σου σάπφειρον.“ τὸν μὲν οὖν παρὰ Πλάτωνι ἀλληγοροῦντες μῦθον οἱ σεμνότερον τὰ τοῦ φιλοσόφου ἐξειληφότες διηγοῦνται. τὰς δὲ προφητείας. ἀφ᾿ ὧν στοχαζόμεθα καὶ τὸν Πλάτωνα εἰληφέναι, οἱ συγγενῶς τοῖς προφήταις καὶ ἐνθέως βιώσαντες καὶ πάντα τὸν χρόνον ἀναθέντες τῇ ἐξετάσει τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων τοῖς ἐπιτηδείοις διὰ βίου καθαρότητα καὶ τὴν περὶ τὰ θεῖα φιλομάθειαν παραστήσουσιν. ἡμῖν δὲ προκείμενον ἦν δεῖξαι ὅτι ἡμεῖς μὲν οὐκ ἀπὸ Ἑλλήνων ἢ Πλάτωνος τὰ περὶ τῆς ἁγίας γῆς εἰλήφαμεν· ἐκεῖνοι δὲ, νεώτεροι γενόμενοι οὐ μόνον τοῦ ἀρχαιοτάτου Μω(??)σέως ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν πλείστων προφητῶν. ἤτοι παρακηκόασί τινων αἰνισσομένων περὶ τῶν τοιούτων, ἢ καὶ ταῖς ἱεραῖς ἐντυχόντες γραφαῖς παραποιήσαντες αὐτὰ τοιαῦτά τινα περὶ τῆς κρείττονος εἰρήκασι γῆς. σαφῶς δ᾿ ὁ Ἀγγαῖος παρίστησιν ἄλλο μὲν εἶναι „τὴν ξηρὰν“ ἄλλο δὲ „τὴν γῆν,“ ξηρὰν καλῶν ταύτην, ἐφ᾿ ᾗ ἐσμεν. λέγει δὲ οὕτως· „ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ (τὴν) γῆν καὶ τὴν ξηρὰν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν.“
pass_a_gloss: It seems (δοκεῖ) to me that also the things about the stones (λίθοι) here thought precious (τίμιοι), said to have a certain effluence (ἀπορροή) from the stones in the better (κρείττων) earth, were taken (λαμβάνω) by Plato from what is written up (ἀναγράφω) in Isaiah about the city (πόλις) of God, about which it is written: ‘I will set your battlements (ἐπάλξεις) jasper (ἴασπις) and your stones stones of crystal (κρύσταλλος) and your enclosure (περίβολος) choice (ἐκλεκτοί) stones’, and again ‘I will set your foundations (θεμέλια) sapphire (σάπφειρος)’. The myth (μῦθος) in Plato, then, those who have taken (ἐκλαμβάνω) the philosopher’s matters more solemnly (σεμνότερον) narrate, allegorizing (ἀλληγορέω). But the prophecies (προφητεῖαι), from which we conjecture (στοχάζομαι) Plato too to have taken, those who lived akin (συγγενῶς) to the prophets and inspired (ἐνθέως) and devoted (ἀνατίθημι) all their time to the examination (ἐξέτασις) of the sacred writings (ἱερὰ γράμματα) will present (παρίστημι) to the fit (ἐπιτήδειοι) through purity (καθαρότης) of life and love of learning (φιλομάθεια) about divine things. Our proposal (προκείμενον) was to show that we did not take from Greeks or Plato the things about the holy land; but they, having come later (νεώτεροι) not only than most ancient Moses but also than most of the prophets, either misheard (παρακούω) some speaking in riddles (αἰνίσσομαι) about such things, or, having encountered (ἐντυγχάνω) the sacred scriptures, altering (παραποιέω) them (αὐτά, neuter: the matters, not the feminine γραφαί), have said some such things about the better earth. Clearly Haggai presents that ‘the dry (ξηρά)’ is one thing and ‘the earth’ another, calling dry this on which we are. He says thus: ‘yet once (ἔτι ἅπαξ) I will shake (σείω) the heaven and the earth and the dry and the sea.’
pass_b_english: It seems to me that what Plato says about the stones thought precious here, which are said to have a kind of outflow from the stones in the better earth, was also taken from what is recorded in Isaiah about the city of God. Of that city it is written: “I will make your battlements jasper, and your stones stones of crystal, and your enclosing wall choice stones” (Isaiah 54:12); and again, “I will make your foundations sapphire” (Isaiah 54:11).

Now those who have taken the philosopher’s words in a loftier sense expound the myth in Plato allegorically. As for the prophecies, from which we conjecture that Plato too borrowed, they will be explained by those who have lived as kin to the prophets and filled with God, and who have given all their time to the study of the sacred writings; and they will explain them to those who are fitted for it by purity of life and by love of learning about divine things.

Our own aim was to show that we did not take what we say about the holy land from the Greeks or from Plato. They, rather, being later not only than Moses, the most ancient of all, but also than most of the prophets, either misheard certain people who spoke in riddles about such things, or else came upon the sacred Scriptures and, altering what they found on these matters, said things of this kind about the better earth. Haggai shows clearly that “the dry land” is one thing and “the earth” another, giving the name dry land to this ground on which we are. He speaks thus: “Once more I will shake the heaven and the earth and the dry land and the sea” (Haggai 2:6).

choices.choice: Isaiah 54:12 LXX reads ‘your gates (πύλας) stones of crystal’; Origen’s text has ‘your stones (τοὺς λίθους)’, translated as he gives it. ‘Your foundations sapphire’ is Isaiah 54:11. Haggai 2:6 LXX has ‘the sea and the dry land’; Origen’s order (dry land before sea) is kept; (τήν) before γῆν is Koetschau’s supplement. Plato’s passage on precious stones as fragments of the stones of the true earth is Phaedo 110d–e; it is described, not quoted, so no inline citation is given. The staged source shows a damaged form ‘Μω(??)σέως’; the word is plainly Μωϋσέως (‘Moses’) and is translated so. ἐνθέως βιώσαντες rendered ‘lived ... filled with God’ (inspired life), not ‘lived piously’. παραποιήσαντες αὐτά: the neuter αὐτά refers to the teachings about the holy land, not to the (feminine) Scriptures, so the English says ‘altering what they found on these matters’; the verb can carry ‘falsified’.
Wrong object fixed: ‘came upon the sacred Scriptures, altered them’ implied the Greeks altered the Scriptures; neuter αὐτά refers to the matters, now ‘altering what they found on these matters’

‘allegorize the myth in Plato and expound it’ (one participle split into two verbs) tightened to ‘expound the myth in Plato allegorically’; ‘teaching’ to ‘words’ for τὰ τοῦ φιλοσόφου, ‘more reverent’ to ‘loftier’ for σεμνότερον
‘set forth’ (twice) to ‘explain’ for παραστήσουσιν; ‘in kinship with the prophets and as men filled with God’ smoothed to ‘as kin to the prophets and filled with God’
Marked the contrastive δέ with ‘Our own aim’
Isaiah 54:11–12 and Haggai 2:6 checked against LXX wording
